  6. Fix: Re-quantize with representative calibration data; try 8-bit (FP8/INT8) for a smaller cost cut; keep a split fleet: quantized 70B for English general chat, bf16 or 8-bit for Hindi and code. Cost math: all-bf16 is 8 GPUs; mixed fleet might be 2 GPUs (70% traffic) plus 4 GPUs (30%) - decide using measured throughput. (Deep serving details in C2.)
  7. Prevention: Stratified eval gate (language, task, length) with per-slice thresholds before any precision change; canary dashboards sliced the same way.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not average slices into one score; I'd not declare victory on latency and cost while ignoring a revenue-relevant segment.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Business insists on cost cuts → Quantify the cost of 7 points of code failures versus savings; use routing.
  • Could a smaller bf16 model be better than a 4-bit large one? → Possible; test, since the trade is task-dependent.
  • Does quantizing the KV cache have the same risk? → Similar: test on long-context and precision tasks.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An int4 rollout looked clean on a general benchmark and then failed on customers' non-English legal text; a slice-aware gate became part of the release checklist.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Accepts or rejects wholesale.
  • Hire: Slices the evaluation and routes regressed traffic to the larger precision.
  • Strong hire: Re-calibrates quantization, compares bit widths, builds stratified gates and a mixed fleet cost model.

questions.contextHtml: A product manager for a medication-information chatbot writes the requirement: "The bot must never hallucinate." The bot answers from a licensed drug database with RAG, serves 30k questions/day, and a pilot review found 1.4% of answers had an unsupported claim (for example a wrong dosage interval). Legal is nervous. You must reply in the requirements meeting.
questions.promptHtml: How do you respond and what do you build?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "We'll make sure it never does" (impossible promise), or "all LLMs hallucinate, can't be fixed."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which errors matter: dosage, contraindication, vs phrasing? What is an acceptable rate per class? Who can the bot refuse or escalate to? Do users see sources?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restrict the pilot: abstain on dosage or interaction questions unless a database passage is quoted verbatim, and add a clear "consult a pharmacist" handoff.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) retrieval misses the correct monograph; (b) model blends adjacent passages (similar drugs); (c) model adds fluent unsupported detail; (d) outdated data.
  4. How I'd verify each: Labelled set of 500 questions with spans; measure retrieval hit rate, groundedness per claim (via claim extraction and entailment checks), and error severity; read the 1.4% by category.
  5. Root cause: Next-token generation optimizes plausibility, not truth; grounding reduces but cannot eliminate unsupported claims. So "never" is not a testable requirement; "severe unsupported claims below X with abstention and verification" is.
  6. Fix: Rewrite the requirement as measurable targets (for example: dosage statements must be quoted from the source; target severe error under 0.1% on the eval with a confidence interval; abstain otherwise). Build: structured retrieval by drug ID, verbatim quoting for critical fields, groundedness verifier, citation display, human review sampling, and an escalation path. Note that proving 0.1% with confidence needs thousands of samples; 3 errors in 3,000 gives roughly an upper bound near 0.3% (rule of three), so size the eval to the claim.
  7. Prevention: Continuous sampling, incident intake, versioned data updates, red-team questions.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: More abstention reduces helpfulness; measure coverage vs error. I'd not promise zero, and I'd not let legal sign-off rest on the model's self-reported confidence.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Can we use temperature 0? → Reduces variance, not unsupported content.
  • Could a second model check the first? → Helpful, but verifier errors exist; combine with deterministic checks on numbers.
  • What about the 1.4%? → Break down by severity; a wrong brand name differs from a wrong dose.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A bot stopped generating dosage text and instead displayed the source table verbatim with a citation; usage stayed high and severe errors disappeared.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Promises zero or says nothing can be done.
  • Hire: Reframes into measurable targets with abstention and grounding.
  • Strong hire: Adds severity classes, verbatim critical fields, sample-size statistics and an escalation design.

questions.promptHtml: An LLM feature starts giving worse answers. How do you decide whether the problem is the model, the prompt, retrieval, tokenization, the context, or the sampling setup?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The best signal of a senior engineer is a structured debugging order that uses cheap, discriminating experiments instead of guessing.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I first find out what changed and for whom, then isolate layers by replaying the exact logged request. I check the final rendered prompt and token counts (truncation, template, tokenizer), then the retrieved context, then rerun with fixed sampling against pinned model versions. Each step rules out a layer. Only after inputs are proven correct do I blame the model, and then I compare against a previous version on a golden set.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
symptom -> scope (which users/languages/lengths/time?) -> change log
   |
   v
1 Request integrity : rendered prompt = intended? chat template, BOS, system prompt, truncation, finish_reason
2 Token accounting  : counted with serving tokenizer? length near limit? language inflation?
3 Context quality   : retrieved docs correct, fresh, ordered, deduped? position of key facts?
4 Embedding/index   : model ID matches index? norms, metric, threshold?
5 Sampling config   : temperature/top_p/max_tokens/stop changed? non-determinism vs real regression?
6 Model version    : alias moved? replay golden set on old vs new
7 Task difficulty   : input distribution shifted (new language, longer docs)?

Mechanism: an LLM pipeline is a chain of deterministic transformations around a stochastic core; most regressions are in the deterministic parts, which are cheap to test. Replay with the saved request and compare diffs between a good and bad trace. For stochastic variation, run N samples and compare rates, since single outputs mislead.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def triage(trace):
    p = render_prompt(trace)                       # exact bytes sent
    return {
        "tokens": count_tokens(MODEL, p),
        "near_limit": count_tokens(MODEL, p) > 0.9 * CTX,
        "finish": trace.finish_reason,
        "retrieved_ids": trace.doc_ids,
        "sampling": trace.params,
        "model_version": trace.model_version,
    }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Tuning the prompt before checking that the rendered prompt is what you think.
  • Comparing single samples of non-deterministic outputs.
  • Missing that an alias silently moved to a new model.
  • Treating "the model got worse" as the first hypothesis.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What do you log to make this possible? → Rendered prompt, params, model version, retrieved IDs, token usage, finish reason, latency, with privacy controls.
  2. How do you tell a model regression from a data shift? → Replay old traffic on the new model and new traffic on the old model; the one that moves is the cause.
  3. What if you cannot reproduce? → Increase sample size, check time-correlated factors (load, batching), and look at slice-level metrics.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer starts rewriting the prompt. The senior starts with scope and diff, checks the cheap deterministic layers first, and insists on traces and replay.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Incident reviews in LLM products repeatedly end at mundane causes: a changed template, a stale index, a truncated prompt or a moved alias, rarely the model itself.
